title: Python first steps: turtle
summary: Type real Python code instead of snapping blocks, and draw a square, a star and a spiral with a turtle.
materials: Windows laptop with Thonny, a free Python editor with Python built in (a grown-up installs it once in this week's first guide step)
phone with a stopwatch for the physics extra

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop again: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. This week you write real code instead of snapping blocks. You use a turtle, a little arrow that draws a line everywhere it moves.

Ask: what should the turtle draw? Three shapes this week: a square, a five-point star, and a spiral that grows outward.

Imagine before you build. On paper, sketch all three shapes first.

1. For the square, picture the turtle drawing one side, then turning, four times in a row.
2. For the star, picture the turtle drawing a line, then turning by a bigger angle than a square's turn. Five turns in a row make the lines cross into points.
3. For the spiral, picture the turtle drawing a short line, then turning a quarter turn. It repeats with a slightly longer line each time, so the path spreads outward.

Plan the pieces before you open Thonny: how many times each shape repeats, and how much the turtle turns each time. Work out the star's angle yourself.

This week runs over two weeks, about an hour each. Week one ends when the square closes. Week two is the star and the spiral.

Five minutes on the same typing site you have been using. This week practise two things Python leans on heavily: the colon key and the Tab key. Type a few practice lines that end in a colon, like for i in range(4): typed out in full, then press Tab once and type the next line indented, then press Backspace or Shift+Tab to get back to the left edge before typing a line with no indent. Colon then Tab is the whole trick your code leans on this week, so get comfortable reaching for both without looking down.

figure.alt: A nested block, repeat 4 times containing forward 100, next to the same idea written as text: for i in range(4): with an indented line t.forward(100) underneath it. A caption says the colon starts a block and the indent says what is inside it.

items.s: colon starts a block; indent says what's inside it

steps.title: Why text, not blocks
steps.body:
Every block you have snapped together in Scratch or the micro:bit editor could be written instead as a line or two of text. In the micro:bit editor, MakeCode, you can flip a switch and see exactly that: the blocks turn into the same program written out in JavaScript or Python, block for block. Scratch keeps its blocks as blocks and never shows you the text underneath, but the same ideas inside those blocks, loops, ifs, variables, are there in every text language too, just typed instead of snapped.

Text scales to big programs in a way blocks do not. A small project might use twenty blocks, easy to see on one screen at once. A real program, the kind that runs a website or a game, can be hundreds of thousands of lines long.

Nobody drags hundreds of thousands of blocks around a screen. Typing lines of text, one after another, in files you can search and copy and paste, is what makes a program that big possible to build and to fix.

Every real programming language used to build real software, not just to teach beginners, is written as text, not blocks. Python is one of those languages, and it needs its own rules for showing what is inside what, since there are no block shapes left to snap together.

A colon at the end of a line tells Python a new block is about to start. Indenting the lines under it, moving them in from the left edge, tells Python which lines belong inside that block. Colons and indents together are how Python reads structure that a block language would have shown with shape alone.

steps.title: Install Thonny and meet its window

figure.alt: A mock of the Thonny window. At the top left, the green Run button. Under it, the big editor where you type. At the bottom, the Shell, where printed numbers and error messages show. Beside the Thonny window, a separate window called Python Turtle Graphics, where the turtle draws. A note says to save the file as shapes.py, never turtle.py.

items.s: Thonny: type, run, then look in two places

steps.body:
This week you type real Python on the laptop itself, in a free editor called Thonny. Thonny comes with Python built in, needs no account and no internet once it is installed, and it is where every turtle drawing this week happens.

For a grown-up, once:

1. Go to https://thonny.org. Near the top right, next to `Download version`, point at `Windows`: a list of files drops down. Click the installer marked `recommended for you`; on most laptops that is the one ending `-x64.exe`. Not the `portable` one.
2. Run the downloaded file. If Windows asks whether to let it run, check it came from thonny.org before saying yes.
3. When the installer asks, pick `Install for me only`: it needs no administrator password.
4. Keep the default choices, click `Next` and then `Install`, and click `Finish` at the end.

For you:

1. Open Thonny from the Start menu.
2. The very first time, it asks for a language and initial settings: pick `English` and `Standard`, then click `Let's go!`.
3. Find the three parts in the figure: the editor at the top, where you type; the `Shell` at the bottom, where printed numbers and error messages appear; and the green `Run` button in the toolbar.
4. In the editor, type `print("hello")`.
5. Click `File`, then `Save`. Make a new folder called `python` in Documents, and save the file there as `hello.py`.
6. Click the green `Run` button.

What you should see: `hello` appears in the `Shell` at the bottom of the window.

If it does not work:

1. A save box opens when you click `Run`: a new file has to be saved before it runs; save it as `hello.py` and it runs.
2. The `Shell` shows an error instead of `hello`: check both quotation marks and both round brackets are there, then click `Run` again.
3. Thonny is not in the Start menu: the install did not finish; the grown-up runs the installer again.

The official guide to the turtle you use next is at https://docs.python.org/3/library/turtle.html. You do not need it yet; it is where to look things up later.

You are done when: the `Shell` says hello, because your own line of Python told it to.

figure.alt: A five-pointed star path the turtle draws, forward 100 along each edge and a turn of 144 degrees at each point, so five turns add up to 720 degrees. Small notes compare it to the square's four 90 degree turns and the spiral's 90 degree turn with a step that grows by 5 each time.

frames.caption: and again at the next point

steps.title: Type turtle code in Thonny
steps.body:
Getting ready:

1. Thonny is the Python editor you set up in Install Thonny and meet its window. It runs your code on this laptop, with no website and no account.
2. Every indented line lines up exactly four spaces in from the left edge, under the line above it. After a line that ends in a colon, Thonny moves the next line in for you.

Draw the square:

1. Open Thonny, click `File`, then `New`.
2. Click `File`, then `Save`, and save it as `shapes.py` in your `python` folder. Never call it `turtle.py`: Python would find your file instead of the real turtle, and nothing would draw.
3. Type `import turtle` on the first line.
4. Type `t = turtle.Turtle()` on the next line.
5. Type `for i in range(4):` on the next line.
6. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `t.forward(100)`.
7. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `t.right(90)`.
8. On the next line, at the left edge with no spaces in front, type `turtle.done()`. It keeps the drawing window open until you close it, so it always stays the very last line: everything you add later goes above it.
9. Click the green `Run` button. A window called `Python Turtle Graphics` opens, and the turtle draws in it. Check it draws a closed square, turning 90 degrees at each corner. Close the drawing window before you run it again.

Good place to stop: the square closes, so this is the end of week one of this quest; the rest is next week. Click `File`, then `Save`, so `shapes.py` stays on the laptop. When you come back, open Thonny; it usually reopens `shapes.py` by itself, and if it does not, click `File`, then `Open`, and pick it. Week two starts at the star.

Draw the star:

Write it yourself first: five lines of 100, each followed by the same turn, and the angle is yours to work out. Give it a real, focused 15 minutes before you use the steps below.

1. Predict first: a square's four 90-degree turns add up to 360, and a star's five turns must add to 720. What angle, repeated 5 times, makes 720?
2. Put the cursor at the very start of the `turtle.done()` line and press Enter, so your new lines go above it.
3. On the empty line above `turtle.done()`, type `for i in range(5):`.
4. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `t.forward(100)`.
5. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `t.right(144)`.
6. Run it and check your answer against 144: the lines should cross into five points.

Draw the spiral:

Write it yourself first: 30 lines with a quarter turn after each, the first line 10 long and every line 5 longer than the one before. Give it a real, focused 15 minutes before you use the steps below.

1. Above `turtle.done()` again, type `step = 10` on its own line.
2. Type `for i in range(30):` on the next line.
3. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `t.forward(step)`.
4. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `print(step)`.
5. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `t.right(90)`.
6. Make sure the next line starts four spaces in (the editor may do this for you), and type `step = step + 5`.
7. Run it and check the path spreads outward instead of closing into a square.
8. Look for the printed numbers in the `Shell` at the bottom of Thonny: 10, 15, 20, and so on up to 155, one for every trip around the loop.

`print` is how programmers look inside a loop. The turtle only shows you the drawing; `print(step)` shows you the number the loop really used each time. It is print what it sees, the habit from the bug diaries, in Python. If a loop ever does something strange, print the variable inside it before you guess.

What you should see: the square closes back to its own corner, four sides and four right-angle turns. The star's five lines cross into five points once the turn is 144 degrees. The spiral spreads outward instead of closing, and the `Shell` at the bottom of Thonny lists the printed step values, one per trip through the loop: 10, 15, 20, and so on.

If it does not work:

1. The `Shell` says `SyntaxError`, often `expected ':'`, at the `for` line: the colon at the end of it is missing. Every `for i in range(...)` line needs a colon before you press Enter.
2. The `Shell` says `IndentationError`, or the lines run outside the loop or the wrong number of times: a line is not lined up under the `for` line by exactly four spaces; check every line meant to be inside the loop starts at the same indent.
3. The `Shell` says `NameError: name 'Step' is not defined`: a capital letter is wrong somewhere, like `Step` instead of `step`; Python treats those as two different names, so match the case exactly everywhere you use it.
4. The drawing window says Not Responding, or the `Shell` says the process ended: close the drawing window, click the red `Stop` button in Thonny's toolbar, then click `Run` again; check `turtle.done()` is the very last line, at the left edge.

You are done when: the spiral draws itself outward in the `Python Turtle Graphics` window, and the `Shell` shows every step value from 10 up to 155.
checklist: The square runs and closes into four sides using a for loop that repeats 4 times
The star runs and shows five points, using t.right(144) inside a loop that repeats 5 times
The spiral runs and spreads outward, using a variable named step that starts at 10 and grows by 5 each trip through the loop
Every line meant to run inside a loop is indented four spaces under its for line, not lined up with the for line itself
I wrote down, in the bug diary, why 144 degrees makes a star, before I typed it

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
Typing code instead of snapping blocks means new kinds of mistakes are possible, ones a block language would not even let you make. Three show up constantly for beginners.

A missing colon: forgetting the colon at the end of a for line. Python needs that colon to know a new block is starting, and without it, the very next line confuses it.

A wrong indent: a line that should be inside the loop typed back at the left edge, or a line that should be outside the loop typed with extra spaces in front of it. Python uses the indent itself to decide what is inside the loop, so an indent in the wrong place changes what the program actually does, even if every word is spelled right.

A capital letter where Python expects a lowercase one, or the other way round: Turtle with a capital T is the name of the turtle tool itself, but a variable you name yourself, like step or t, is whatever case you typed it, and Python treats step and Step as two completely different names.

When the code breaks, Python prints an error message, often several lines long. Read it from the bottom line first, not the top. The bottom line usually names the actual problem in plain words, while the lines above it just show which line was running when it broke. Write down, in your bug diary, one real error you hit today, what the bottom line of the message said, and what you changed to fix it. Also write down how you worked out the star's angle, and what happened if you tried a wrong guess before landing on 144.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of your three shapes on screen, the square, the star and the spiral, and the code you typed for the spiral, copied out or screenshotted.

extras.title: Draw a hexagon
extras.body:
Use the same loop pattern to draw a shape with six sides instead of four or five.

1. Open Thonny. If `shapes.py` is not already open, click `File`, then `Open`, and pick it.
2. Add a new `for i in range(6):` loop below your existing shapes, above `turtle.done()`.
3. Predict first: six turns must add up to 360 degrees. What angle, repeated six times, makes 360?
4. Indent the next line and type `t.forward(80)`.
5. Indent the next line and type `t.right(60)`.
6. Run it and check the shape closes into a six-sided hexagon.

What to notice: as the number of sides goes up, the turn angle goes down.

extras.title: Give each shape its own colour
extras.body:
Add colour to your turtle so each shape stands out from the others.

1. Open Thonny. If `shapes.py` is not already open, click `File`, then `Open`, and pick it.
2. Right after `t = turtle.Turtle()`, type `t.pencolor("blue")`.
3. Before your star loop, type `t.pencolor("red")`.
4. Before your spiral loop, type `t.pencolor("green")`.
5. Run the program and check each shape now draws in its own colour.

What to notice: the colour only changes what is drawn after that line, not lines drawn earlier.

extras.title: Draw a shape of your own
extras.body:
What shape, sign or pattern do you want to teach the turtle to draw?

Design your own shape using a loop, the way this week's shapes worked.

It must use a `for` loop and a colon, the way this week's shapes did.
It must have one number you choose by testing, like the number of sides or the angle.
It must be shown running to someone in your house, with the code visible.

Sketch it on paper and work out the angle yourself first.

How to know it works: the shape on screen matches your sketch closely enough that someone recognizes it.

extras.title: How many flips make it look smooth?
extras.body:
Find out how many flips each second your own flipbook needs before the drawing looks like it is truly moving.

1. Predict first: guess the number of flips each second where the pictures will start to look like smooth motion instead of separate drawings. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Draw 10 simple pictures on paper corners, each one a small step further than the last, like a bouncing ball.
3. Flip through them slowly with a phone stopwatch running, and time how many seconds 10 flips take.
4. Flip through them as fast as you can, timing 10 flips again.
5. Divide 10 by each time in seconds to get flips per second for both speeds.

Compare: at which speed did the motion look smooth, and was that close to your prediction?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why separate drawings can look like one smooth motion when they flip by fast enough.

extras.title: Turn a turtle all the way around the world
extras.body:
Find out how the turtle's own turns connect to the size of the real Earth.

1. Write a short turtle program that turns 1 degree and moves forward a tiny step, 360 times in a loop, with `turtle.done()` as its last line.
2. Run it and watch the turtle trace a full circle back to where it started.
3. Look up or recall that the Earth's circumference at the equator is about 40,075 kilometres.
4. Divide 40,075 by 360 to find how many kilometres one degree covers on the real Earth.

What to notice: a full turn is 360 degrees for a turtle on screen and for the planet itself. On Earth's equator each one of those degrees is about 111 kilometres.
